```{r options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", error = FALSE)
```

The [first tutorial](biocroxytest.html) checks that selecting samples preserves
the requested order. A Bioconductor function may receive an ordinary matrix
or an HDF5-backed assay. We want the same behavior from both, with one shared
set of assertions.

This tutorial uses the GitHub development version, testthat 3.3.0 or newer,
SummarizedExperiment and HDF5Array. See the first tutorial's installation block.
It starts with a fresh copy; no objects from another article are required.

## Prepare the two cases

```{r prepare-package}
template <- system.file("examples", "samplealignment", package = "biocroxytest",
                        mustWork = TRUE)
pkg <- tempfile("samplealignment-")
fs::dir_copy(template, pkg)
source_file <- file.path(pkg, "R", "align-samples.R")
named_source <- system.file("examples", "steps", "named-cases.R",
                            package = "biocroxytest", mustWork = TRUE)
file.copy(named_source, source_file, overwrite = TRUE)
withr::with_dir(pkg, biocroxytest::use_longtests())
writeLines("^\\.BBSoptions$", file.path(pkg, ".Rbuildignore"))
```

The copy command replaces the first tutorial's `@tests` block with the
following complete file. In your own package, you would edit the R source
directly. `use_longtests()` creates the separate runner and enables
`RunLongTests: TRUE` in `.BBSoptions`, preserving an existing runner.
The final line keeps this build-system setting out of the example's source
tarball. In an existing package, append that pattern to `.Rbuildignore`
instead of replacing its other entries.

```{r named-source, code=readLines(source_file), eval=FALSE}
```

Read the declaration in three parts:

- **`sample-alignment`** names the group. Combined with each case name it
  gives the stable IDs `sample-alignment/memory` and `sample-alignment/hdf5`.
- **`setup`** creates the input for each case. The HDF5 case writes a real
  backing file, checks its class and cleans it up after the test with withr.
- **`test`** runs the same three assertions for each input. The expected
  sample names, counts and conditions are written explicitly.

The memory case belongs to the ordinary suite. The HDF5 case goes into
`longtests` so it can run separately with its backend dependency. This tiny
example is fast: HDF5 does not automatically make a test slow, and you can
put both cases in the ordinary suite if that suits your package.

For a standalone long test with no shared assertions, use an `@longtests`
block instead of `@tests` and enable the suite with `use_longtests()`.
Named cases are useful when you want to reuse a test body or select a case by ID.

## Generate and inspect the plan

```{r generate, message=FALSE}
roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg)
plan <- biocroxytest::test_case_plan(pkg)
plan[c("id", "suite")]
```

You should see two rows, one for each ID and its chosen suite. Planning reads
the declarations without running the setup or creating an HDF5 file.
Moving a case to another source file or suite does not change its ID.

The generated files are:

| Case | Generated file |
| --- | --- |
| memory | `tests/testthat/test-roxytest-tests-align-samples.R` |
| hdf5 | `longtests/testthat/test-biocroxytest-longtests-align-samples.R` |

They run with standard testthat. From an R session you can run both source suites:

```{r run-suites, message=FALSE}
ordinary <- testthat::test_local(pkg, reporter = "silent")
long <- testthat::test_dir(file.path(pkg, "longtests", "testthat"),
                           package = "samplealignment", load_package = "source",
                           reporter = "silent")
rbind(ordinary = as.data.frame(ordinary)[c("failed", "error", "passed")],
      long = as.data.frame(long)[c("failed", "error", "passed")])
```

Each suite should pass four expectations: one for the input backend and three
for the selected samples. For an installed package check, use
`R CMD check package_version.tar.gz` and
`R CMD check --test-dir=longtests package_version.tar.gz` in separate output
directories. Each suite must have its own helpers; it must not rely on the
other suite having run first.

```{r verify-suites, include=FALSE}
for (result in list(ordinary, long)) {
  summary <- as.data.frame(result)
  stopifnot(sum(summary$passed) == 4L, sum(summary$failed) == 0L, !any(summary$error))
}
```

## Run just one case

During development, select the case you are working on:

```{r select-case, message=FALSE}
biocroxytest::run_test_case("sample-alignment/hdf5", path = pkg)
```

This runs the selected generated test with its suite's helpers. Regenerate
with `roxygen2::roxygenise(pkg)` whenever you change the case declaration.
Use a full suite run for custom runners or tests that depend on earlier tests.

## Record whether both cases completed

Use `run_test_plan()` when you want a structured report. It runs each case in
its own R session and temporary package copy, so each result has an execution
context. This is optional; ordinary testthat runs remain the basic workflow.

```{r evidence, message=FALSE}
ids <- c("sample-alignment/memory", "sample-alignment/hdf5")
evidence <- biocroxytest::run_test_plan(pkg, ids = ids, seed = 42L)
evidence$cases[c("id", "suite", "status")]
biocroxytest::check_test_plan(evidence, required = ids)
```

Both statuses should be `completed`. A passing assertion followed by a skip
does not count as complete. `check_test_plan()` requires both IDs to complete
without recorded warnings, and raises an error otherwise. This can make a
backend case mandatory in CI instead of silently accepting a skip.

```{r cleanup, include=FALSE}
unloadNamespace("samplealignment")
unlink(pkg, recursive = TRUE)
```
